steps.tx: Nutritional **scurvy** is a metabolic bone and collagen disorder resulting from severe ascorbic acid (Vitamin C) deficiency. Ascorbic acid acts as an essential cofactor for prolyl and lysyl hydroxylase enzymes, which hydroxylate proline and lysine residues during procollagen synthesis. Without hydroxylation, defective tropocollagen triple helices cannot cross-link, compromising capillary basement membranes and osteoid formation throughout the growing skeleton.
steps.say: Scurvy is caused by severe vitamin C deficiency. Ascorbic acid is a required cofactor for prolyl and lysyl hydroxylase to build strong collagen. Without it, collagen triple helices cannot cross-link. This leads to fragile capillaries that hemorrhage and defective bone osteoid that cannot support mechanical stress.

steps.tx: Infantile scurvy presents characteristically between six and twenty-four months of age with severe limb tenderness causing **scorbutic pseudoparalysis**. Because massive subperiosteal hemorrhages strip the sensitive periosteum, the infant lies motionless in a pithecoid or frog-leg posture with hips and knees semi-flexed and externally rotated, screaming upon the slightest touch. Bleeding around erupting teeth produces purple, spongy, swollen gums.
steps.say: Infants between six and twenty-four months present with scorbutic pseudoparalysis. Bleeding under the periosteum causes agonizing pain, so the baby refuses to move and lies in a frog-leg posture, crying whenever touched. If teeth have erupted, you will see purple, bleeding, swollen gums.

left.title: Scurvy Pseudoparalysis
points: Bilateral lower limbs held in frog-leg posture
Normal deep tendon reflexes when calmed
Swollen, purple, bleeding gums over teeth

right.title: True Paralysis Mimics
points: Septic arthritis: hot, red, monoarticular joint
Obstetric brachial palsy: presents at birth

steps.tx: The pathognomonic radiographic sign is the **white line of Fraenkel**, representing a dense, thickened zone of provisional calcification at the metaphyseal margin. In scurvy, calcification of cartilaginous matrix proceeds normally, but osteoblasts fail to deposit osteoid and osteoclasts fail to resorb the calcified cartilage. This dense, brittle transverse white line caps the metaphysis like an unyielding plate.
steps.say: Look for the white line of Fraenkel on radiographs of the knees. It is a dense, thick transverse white band capping the metaphysis. In scurvy, cartilage calcification happens normally, but osteoblasts cannot lay down bone on top of it. This leaves a dense, brittle plate of unresorbed calcified cartilage.

vis.title: Cardinal Radiographic Signs of Scurvy
rows: Lateral bony beak or triangular spur
Fractured, displaced margin of Fraenkel line
Sharp circular sclerotic rim with lucent core

steps.tx: Directly adjacent to the Fraenkel line lies the **Trummerfeld zone**, a radiolucent scorbutic band composed of shattered, debris-filled trabeculae and microfractures devoid of collagen. This zone of structural weakness is prone to pathological metaphyseal fracture-separation (epiphysiolysis). Fractured fragments displaced laterally from the white line of Fraenkel form the diagnostic Pelkan spurs at the cortical margins.
steps.say: Directly beneath the Fraenkel line sits the Trummerfeld zone, a dark radiolucent stripe of crushed, broken bone trabeculae. Because it lacks collagen reinforcement, this zone easily fractures and separates. Fragments squeezed out sideways at the edges of the bone form sharp lateral spikes called Pelkan spurs.

right.title: Pelkan Spurs
points: Points away from adjacent growth plate

steps.tx: Definitive management requires oral **ascorbic acid supplementation** administered at doses of one hundred to two hundred and fifty milligrams daily. Clinical improvement is dramatic: irritability and bone pain subside within twenty-four to forty-eight hours, and spontaneous limb movement resumes within days. Subperiosteal hematomas calcify extensively within one to two weeks, producing characteristic calcified cloaks encasing the shaft.
steps.say: Treat scurvy with oral ascorbic acid, one hundred to two hundred and fifty milligrams daily. The recovery is dramatic: bone pain and irritability vanish within forty-eight hours, and the child starts moving their legs again. Within two weeks, X-rays show huge calcifying sleeves around the bones as the subperiosteal hematomas heal.

vis.title: Therapeutic Response Timeline
rows: Pain and irritability resolve; appetite returns
Fraenkel and Trummerfeld zones remodel fully

quiz.q: What is the biochemical cause of capillary fragility and defective osteoid synthesis in scurvy?
options: Deficiency of ascorbic acid as a cofactor for prolyl and lysyl hydroxylase
Inability of alkaline phosphatase to cleave inorganic pyrophosphate
Defective 1-alpha-hydroxylation of vitamin D in the renal tubules
Excessive osteoclast activation mediated by parathyroid hormone
quiz.explain: Ascorbic acid is the required reducing cofactor for prolyl and lysyl hydroxylase enzymes; deficiency impairs collagen triple-helix stabilization, causing capillary and osteoid fragility.

quiz.q: Which radiographic sign in scurvy describes a sharp circular sclerotic outline around an osteopenic epiphyseal center?
quiz.explain: The Wimberger ring sign is the sharp, thin circular radiopaque margin surrounding a radiolucent, osteopenic epiphyseal ossification center in scurvy.
